passages.happening:
Paul speaks to slaves. “All who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited” (verse 1).

“Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, since those receiving their good service are beloved believers. Teach and encourage these principles” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world. Slaves worked in houses, fields, mines and workshops; some were trusted managers, teachers or doctors, others did crushing labour. People became slaves through war, through being born to an enslaved mother, through debt, or by being abandoned as babies. Roman slavery was not based on race, and many slaves in the cities could hope to be freed one day. But by law a slave was property. A slave could be bought and sold, beaten, separated from family and used sexually by the master.

The church in Ephesus had slaves and masters in it, sometimes from the same household, sitting together and hearing this letter read. Notice what the slaves heard. They were spoken to directly, as people who answer to God. And the reason Paul gives is not that masters deserve it, but that God's name and the gospel should not be mocked by outsiders.

Verse 2 deals with a new question. If a slave and his master were now both believers, ‘brothers’, should the slave stop working well? Paul says no: serve them all the more, because they too are ‘beloved believers’. Notice the word ‘brothers’. In Christ the master and the slave are family. That word, said in front of both, was itself a crack in the wall between them.
passages.ot:
The God of Israel shows no favouritism: “For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17).

Job says why he could not mistreat his own servants: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15).

Israel's law told masters, “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 25:43), and reminded them, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (Deuteronomy 15:15). It made kidnapping a person a capital crime (Exodus 21:16), and said, “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you” (Deuteronomy 23:15).
passages.hard:
Why does Paul tell slaves to honour their masters instead of condemning slavery? Paul does not command the end of slavery here, and that should not be softened. He writes to a small, powerless movement in an empire where slavery was everywhere and slave revolts were crushed with great violence. His stated concern is that God's name and the gospel not be discredited.

But within that world he does what ordinary household rules did not. He speaks to slaves as people who answer to God. He calls believing masters and slaves ‘brothers’. Elsewhere he tells masters that they have a Master in heaven, with no favouritism (Ephesians 6:9). In this very letter he names ‘slave traders’ among the lawbreakers (1:10). On the most common reading of a debated verse, he tells slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and he asks Philemon to take back Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). Many readers see in this the seeds of the truth that would undo slavery: every person bears God's image, and in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

The history of verses like these is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used them to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical, while they ignored the equality of all in Christ. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Atlantic slavery, built on race and kidnapping, was very different from the Roman kind, and the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death. Christians who opposed slavery drew on the same Bible, on human dignity, the exodus and the gospel. The church's record was mixed, and it must be named honestly.

Nor are these verses a simple rule for employment today. A worker is not property, and a boss is not an owner. Some of what Paul says, to work honestly and with respect, can be applied to work with care. But no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work.

The Honest Answer ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’ goes further.
passages.asks: Paul tells believing slaves and masters that they are brothers. Ask whom you treat as beneath you, at work, at home or in church. If you have power over others, ask whether you treat them as family in Christ. And ask whether you see the people who serve you as Christ sees them.

passages.t: Godliness is not a means of gain
passages.happening:
Paul turns back to the false teachers. Anyone who teaches otherwise “is conceited and understands nothing. Instead, he has an unhealthy interest in controversies and semantics” (verse 4), which breed envy, quarrels and suspicion. “These men regard godliness as a means of gain” (verse 5).

“Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these” (verses 6-8).

“Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Travelling teachers in the Greek world often charged fees, and some were mocked as sellers of wisdom who were in it for the money. The false teachers in Ephesus seem to have fit that pattern. They loved arguments over words, and they treated religion as a way to make money.

Paul turns their own word around. They wanted ‘gain’. Paul says godliness is great gain, but only ‘with contentment’. Philosophers of the time, especially the Stoics, prized a word for contentment that meant needing little, being self-sufficient. Paul uses the same word but gives it a different root. Contentment does not come from the self. It comes from God, who gives food and clothing, and from remembering that we brought nothing into the world and will take nothing out.

Then comes the warning. ‘Those who want to be rich’ are walking into a trap. The pictures are strong: ensnared, plunged, pierced. Wanting more can drown a person.

Verse 10 is one of the most quoted verses in the Bible, and one of the most misquoted. It is not ‘money is the root of all evil’. Paul does not say money is evil, or that it is the only root of evil. He says the love of money is a root from which every kind of evil can grow. The word he uses means fondness for silver. And he aims it at people who wanted to be rich, some of them religious teachers. Anyone can crave money, and Paul says that craving has led people away from the faith and into many sorrows.
passages.ot:
Job said it first: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return” (Job 1:21). The Teacher agreed: “He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands” (Ecclesiastes 5:15). And a psalm warns, “For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down” (Psalm 49:17).

Proverbs warns against the race for riches: “Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself” (Proverbs 23:4). It praises contentment: “Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil” (Proverbs 15:16). And it prays for enough: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion” (Proverbs 30:8).
passages.hard:
Does God promise that faith or giving will make you rich?

No. These notes say so plainly. Some teachers say that if you have enough faith, or give to God or to their ministry, God will pay you back with more money or better health. This is often called prosperity teaching, or the prosperity gospel. It is one of the things this site does not teach as true. It is the very thing Paul warns about here: treating godliness ‘as a means of gain’. Many who teach it are sincere, and many who believe it are hoping for help in hard times. They deserve care, not scorn. But it is a mistake.

Paul's own picture is the opposite. Godliness is great gain with contentment. Food and clothing are enough. Those who want to be rich fall into a trap. And in the next verses he tells the rich not to hope in their wealth.

If you gave money because you were pressed or frightened, or because someone promised that God would pay you back, and the return never came, that was not your failure. You were not lacking in faith. The promise was wrong. It may help to talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says godliness with contentment is great gain. Ask what would have to change for you to say ‘food and clothing are enough’. Ask whether you want to be rich, and what that wanting is doing to you. And ask whether you have ever treated your faith as a way to get something from God, rather than as a way to know him.

passages.t: Flee, pursue, fight: the good confession
passages.happening:
“But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good confession before many witnesses” (verses 11-12).

Paul charges Timothy “in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate” (verse 13), to keep the command until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which God will bring about in his own time: “the blessed and only Sovereign One—the King of kings and Lord of lords” (verse 15). “He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
‘Man of God’ was the Old Testament title for Moses, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha and other prophets. Paul places Timothy in that line.

Then three verbs. Flee: run from the love of money and all it brings. Pursue: chase after six good things, the last of them gentleness. Fight: hold your ground in the faith. Christian life is not passive. It runs away, runs toward, and stands firm.

Timothy had ‘made the good confession before many witnesses’, perhaps at his baptism or when he was set apart for his work. Paul links it to another confession: Christ Jesus ‘before Pontius Pilate’. Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from about AD 26 to 36, the official under whom Jesus was crucified. His name was fixed so firmly in the church's memory that it later went into the Apostles' Creed. Jesus told the truth before the most powerful man in the land, and it cost him his life. Timothy is to stand the same way.

Then the letter breaks into praise. The title ‘King of kings and Lord of lords’ had been claimed by great rulers in the ancient world, and Roman emperors received lavish divine titles. Paul gives the title to God alone. He ‘alone is immortal’. No emperor is. No one can see him. And yet the One who cannot be seen has shown himself in Christ Jesus, whose appearing the church waits for.
passages.ot:
‘Man of God’ was said of Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Elijah and Elisha. It names those who speak for God.

God as the King above all kings is the confession of the Old Testament: “For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords” (Deuteronomy 10:17). Even a pagan king said to Daniel, “Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings” (Daniel 2:47).

God dwelling in light that no one can approach is in the Psalms: “He wraps Himself in light as with a garment” (Psalm 104:2). And God told Moses, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20).

And the call to be strong is Joshua's: “Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous? Do not be afraid” (Joshua 1:9).
passages.asks: Paul tells Timothy to flee, pursue and fight. Ask what you need to run from, and what you need to run after. Ask where you have been called to make a good confession, as Jesus did before Pilate, and whether you are standing firm. And ask whether you give God the honour Paul gives him here, as the only King above every king.

passages.t: A word to the rich; guard what has been entrusted
passages.happening:
“Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy. Instruct them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share, treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life” (verses 17-19).

“O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called ‘knowledge,’ which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith. Grace be with you all” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Paul has warned those who want to be rich. Now he speaks to those who already are. He does not tell them they are sinners for having money. He tells them what to do with it.

First, do not be proud, and do not hope in wealth. Riches are ‘uncertain’; they can be gone in a day. Hope belongs in God, ‘who richly provides all things for us to enjoy’. Notice that: God gives good things to be enjoyed, not merely put up with. Paul is no enemy of good gifts.

Second, be ‘rich in good works’, generous and ready to share. In Ephesus, wealthy people were expected to pay for public buildings, festivals and feasts, and in return their names were carved on inscriptions in their honour. Paul turns that around. Give, but not for your name on a stone. Give, and store up treasure for the age to come.

Then Paul's last charge: ‘guard what has been entrusted to you’. The picture is of something valuable left in a friend's safekeeping. The gospel was not Timothy's to change. It was his to keep safe and pass on.

And the last words are for everyone: ‘Grace be with you all.’ The word ‘you’ is plural. The letter was written to Timothy, but the whole church was listening.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament warns against trusting riches: “He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like foliage” (Proverbs 11:28). “If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm 62:10). It reminds the wealthy where wealth comes from: “But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:18).

It honours generosity: “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender” (Proverbs 19:17). And it reminds rich and poor alike who they are: “The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is Maker of them all” (Proverbs 22:2).
passages.hard:
Is it wrong for a Christian to be rich?

Paul does not say so. He tells the rich not to be proud, not to hope in their money, and to be generous. Christians agree that everything a person has comes from God, that greed is a serious sin, that the poor are to be cared for, that generosity belongs to the Christian life, and that wealth is never by itself a sign of God's favour.

Beyond that, they differ. Many read Scripture as allowing believers to own, earn, save and build, as stewards who give generously and refuse to let money rule them. Others, among them monastic orders and many in the Anabaptist tradition, hold that Jesus' words call at least some believers to a deliberately simple life, and call every church to question its comfort. These notes do not choose. The site's wisdom topic on money sets out these views, and the Honest Answer ‘What does the Bible say about money?’ goes further.
passages.asks: Paul tells the rich to hope in God and be rich in good works. Ask, whatever you have, where your hope really rests. Ask what you could give or share this week, not for your name, but because God has given to you. And ask what you have been entrusted with in the faith that you need to guard and pass on.
